problems.title: Set Matrix Zeroes
problems.statement:
Given an `m x n` integer matrix `matrix`, if an element is `0`, set its entire row and column to `0`'s.

You must do it in place and return the modified matrix.

examples.explanation: The 0 in the center clears row 1 and column 1.
Zeros at (0,0) and (0,3) clear row 0, col 0, and col 3.
Single cell with zero remains zero.

commonMistakes: Setting rows and columns to zero immediately during the first traversal, which creates false zeros.
Failing to handle the first row and column flags separately.
hints: Can you use the first row and first column as markers?
Use two separate boolean flags for whether row 0 and col 0 themselves contain zero.
Update the inner matrix first, then update row 0 and col 0 using the flags.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Spiral Matrix
problems.statement: Given an `m x n` `matrix`, return all elements of the `matrix` in spiral order (clockwise starting from the top-left corner).

examples.explanation: Follow top row right, right col down, bottom row left, left col up, then center.

commonMistakes: Double counting elements on single row or single column subgrids when top <= bottom check is omitted.
Index out of bounds on directional turn.
hints: Track 4 boundaries: top, bottom, left, right.
Traverse left-to-right along top, increment top.
Traverse top-to-bottom along right, decrement right.
Before traversing right-to-left along bottom, verify top <= bottom.
Before traversing bottom-to-top along left, verify left <= right.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=10 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1 for complexity verification

problems.title: Spiral Matrix II
problems.statement: Given a positive integer `n`, generate an `n x n` `matrix` filled with elements from `1` to `n^2` in spiral order.
commonMistakes: Using <= in the boundary checks after incrementing top/left without checking val <= n*n.
Off-by-one errors in corner coordinate transitions.
hints: Initialize an n x n 2D array with 0.
Set 4 boundary pointers: top = 0, bottom = n-1, left = 0, right = n-1.
Increment counter from 1 to n*n as you fill along boundaries.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1000 for complexity verification

problems.title: Rotate Image
problems.statement:
You are given an `n x n` 2D `matrix` representing an image, rotate the image by 90 degrees (clockwise).

You have to rotate the image in-place and return the rotated matrix.
commonMistakes: Transposing twice or running inner loop for all j instead of j = i + 1, canceling out the transposition.
Forgetting to reverse rows after transposition.
hints: A 90 degree clockwise rotation is equivalent to transpose + horizontal flip (reverse each row).
Transpose: swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for j > i.
Reverse: for each row, reverse in-place.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=15 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification

problems.title: Transpose Matrix
problems.statement:
Given a 2D integer array `matrix`, return the transpose of `matrix`.

The transpose of a matrix is the matrix flipped over its main diagonal, switching the matrix's row and column indices.
commonMistakes: Assuming the matrix is always square (n x n) and attempting in-place swaps on rectangular matrices.
hints: If matrix is m x n, transposed matrix is n x m.
res[c][r] = matrix[r][c] for all r in [0, m-1] and c in [0, n-1].

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=10 for complexity verification

problems.title: Reshape the Matrix
problems.statement:
In MATLAB, there is a handy function called `reshape` which can reshape an `m x n` matrix into a new one with a different size `r x c` keeping its original data.

You are given an `m x n` matrix `mat` and two integers `r` and `c` representing the number of rows and columns of the wanted reshaped matrix.

The reshaped matrix should be filled with all the elements of the original matrix in the same row-traversing order as they were.

If the `reshape` operation with given parameters is possible and legal, output the new reshaped matrix; Otherwise, output the original matrix.

examples.explanation: Total elements 4 != 8, reshape invalid, returns original matrix.

commonMistakes: Failing to return the original matrix unchanged when m * n !== r * c.
Incorrect index division / modulo mapping.
hints: First check if m * n == r * c. If not, return mat.
Map linear index i from 0 to m*n - 1 to (i / n, i % n) in original and (i / c, i % c) in reshaped.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Game of Life
problems.statement:
According to Conway's Game of Life, the board is an `m x n` grid of cells where each cell is either 0 (dead) or 1 (live).

Each cell interacts with its eight neighbors (horizontal, vertical, diagonal) using four rules:
1. Any live cell with fewer than two live neighbors dies (under-population).
2. Any live cell with two or three live neighbors lives on to the next generation.
3. Any live cell with more than three live neighbors dies (over-population).
4. Any dead cell with exactly three live neighbors becomes a live cell (reproduction).

The next state is created by applying the rules simultaneously to every cell. Return the board after one step.

examples.explanation: Dead cell with 3 live neighbors becomes live.
Single cell has 0 neighbors and dies.

commonMistakes: Updating board cells in-place with 0/1 directly, which corrupts neighbor counts for subsequent cells.
Missing diagonal neighbor checks.
hints: Use bit 0 for current state and bit 1 for next state.
When counting live neighbors, read `board[nr][nc] & 1`.
After processing all cells, shift each cell right by 1 bit: `board[r][c] >>= 1`.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=25 for complexity verification

problems.title: Number of Islands
problems.statement:
Given an `m x n` 2D binary grid `grid` which represents a map of `'1'`s (land) and `'0'`s (water), return the number of islands.

An island is surrounded by water and is formed by connecting adjacent lands horizontally or vertically. You may assume all four edges of the grid are all surrounded by water.

parameterDefinitions.name: grid
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n 2D grid containing '1' and '0'

examples.explanation: All 1s connect into a single large island.

commonMistakes: Checking diagonals (problem states connectivity is strictly horizontal and vertical).
Stack overflow on very large grids without marking cells visited immediately.
hints: Iterate over every cell. When you encounter land ('1'), increment count and trigger DFS/BFS.
Sink the island by converting connected '1's to '0's during traversal.
Ensure string '1' vs number 1 type consistency.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=25 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Max Area of Island
problems.statement:
You are given an `m x n` binary matrix `grid`. An island is a group of `1`'s (representing land) connected 4-directionally (horizontal or vertical).

The area of an island is the number of cells with a value `1` in the island.

Return the maximum area of an island in `grid`. If there is no island, return `0`.

examples.explanation: The maximum island area is 6 cells.
All 4 cells form a single island.

commonMistakes: Failing to mark visited cells before recursing, causing infinite loops.
Returning 1 instead of 0 for empty or all-zero grids.
hints: Use DFS or BFS to traverse each connected component.
Return 1 + sum of DFS calls in all 4 orthogonal directions.
Track the running maximum over all connected components.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=35 for complexity verification

problems.title: Flood Fill
problems.statement:
An image is represented by an `m x n` integer grid `image` where `image[i][j]` represents the pixel value of the image.

You are also given three integers `sr`, `sc`, and `color`. You should perform a flood fill on the image starting from the pixel `image[sr][sc]`.

To perform a flood fill, consider the starting pixel, plus any pixels connected 4-directionally to the starting pixel of the same color as the starting pixel, plus any pixels connected 4-directionally to those pixels (also with the same color), and so on. Replace the color of all of the aforementioned pixels with `color`.

Return the modified image after performing the flood fill.

examples.explanation: All 1s connected to (1,1) are replaced with 2. Bottom right 1 is not connected 4-directionally.
Starting color is already 0, image remains unchanged.

commonMistakes: Failing to check `originalColor === color` at the beginning, leading to infinite recursion or queue overflow.
hints: Store `originalColor = image[sr][sc]`.
If `originalColor === color`, return image immediately.
Otherwise, standard 4-directional DFS/BFS recoloring pixels equal to originalColor.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Surrounded Regions
problems.statement:
Given an `m x n` matrix `board` containing `'X'` and `'O'`, capture all regions that are 4-directionally surrounded by `'X'`.

A region is captured by flipping all `'O'`s into `'X'`s in that surrounded region. Any `'O'` on the border or connected to a border `'O'` cannot be flipped.

Return the modified `board` in-place.

examples.explanation: The 'O' at (3,1) is on the boundary and saved; interior 'O's are flipped to 'X'.

commonMistakes: Trying to identify surrounded regions from the inside out instead of boundary-first traversal.
Forgetting to restore escaped border cells back to 'O'.
hints: Invert the problem: which 'O's CANNOT be captured? Any 'O' connected to the border.
Run DFS/BFS starting from all border cells with value 'O', marking them as safe (e.g. '#').
Flip all remaining 'O's to 'X', and restore '#' back to 'O'.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=25 for complexity verification

problems.title: Pacific Atlantic Water Flow
problems.statement:
There is an `m x n` rectangular island that borders both the Pacific Ocean and Atlantic Ocean. The Pacific Ocean touches the island's left and top edges, and the Atlantic Ocean touches the island's right and bottom edges.

The island is partitioned into a grid of square cells. You are given an `m x n` integer matrix `heights` where `heights[r][c]` represents the height above sea level of the cell at coordinate `(r, c)`.

Rain water can flow to neighboring cells directly north, south, east, and west if the neighboring cell's height is less than or equal to the current cell's height. Water can flow from any cell adjacent to an ocean directly into that ocean.

Return a 2D list of grid coordinates `result` where `result[i] = [ri, ci]` denotes that rain water can flow from cell `(ri, ci)` to both the Pacific and Atlantic oceans (coordinates sorted in row-major order).

examples.explanation: These 7 cells can flow water to both Pacific (top/left) and Atlantic (bottom/right).
Peak cells flow to both oceans.

commonMistakes: Traversing downwards from each cell to ocean (O((mn)^2)), causing TLE.
Flow condition reversed: when flowing inland from ocean, neighbor height must be >= current height.
hints: Reverse the flow: start DFS from ocean borders and flow uphill (heights[nr][nc] >= heights[r][c]).
Pacific starts at row 0 and col 0; Atlantic starts at row m-1 and col n-1.
Intersection of reachable cells in both boolean matrices gives the final answer.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=25 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Rotting Oranges
problems.statement:
You are given an `m x n` `grid` where each cell can have one of three values:
- `0` representing an empty cell,
- `1` representing a fresh orange, or
- `2` representing a rotten orange.

Every minute, any fresh orange that is 4-directionally adjacent to a rotten orange becomes rotten.

Return the minimum number of minutes that must elapse until no cell has a fresh orange. If this is impossible, return `-1`.

examples.explanation: After 4 minutes, all fresh oranges are rotted.
The orange in bottom left corner is isolated and never rots.
No fresh oranges initially, answer is 0.
Fresh orange with no rotten orange never rots.

commonMistakes: Returning minutes incremented even when no fresh oranges were converted.
Forgetting the edge case where initial fresh count is 0.
hints: Multi-source BFS: add all initial rotten oranges to the queue at time 0.
Count the total number of fresh oranges.
Process queue level-by-level (each level = 1 minute). When fresh reaches 0, stop.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=10 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=10 for complexity verification

problems.title: Walls and Gates
problems.statement:
You are given an `m x n` grid `rooms` initialized with these three possible values:
- `-1` A wall or an obstacle.
- `0` A gate.
- `INF` (2147483647) An empty room.

Fill each empty room with the distance to its nearest gate. If it is impossible to reach a gate, it should be filled with `INF`.

Return the modified `rooms` matrix.

examples.explanation: Multi-source BFS from gates fills the shortest distance to each room.
No gate, room unreachable, remains INF.

commonMistakes: Running BFS from each room towards gates instead of multi-source BFS from all gates outwards.
Visiting already reached rooms with equal or smaller distance.
hints: Push all gates (cells with value 0) into a single BFS queue.
When an INF neighbor is reached, its shortest distance is rooms[r][c] + 1.
Push neighbor to queue. Multi-source BFS guarantees optimal distance upon first visit.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=25 for complexity verification

problems.title: 01 Matrix
problems.statement:
Given an `m x n` binary matrix `mat`, return the distance of the nearest `0` for each cell.

The distance between two adjacent cells is `1`.
constraints: There is at least one 0 in mat.

examples.explanation: The distance of 1 in center to nearest 0 is 1.
Bottom center cell has distance 2 to nearest zero.

commonMistakes: Running independent BFS from each 1 cell (O((mn)^2)), causing TLE.
Using array.shift() in BFS on large grids leading to O(N^2) queue operations.
hints: Multi-source BFS: enqueue all 0 cells with distance 0.
When expanding to adjacent cells, set dist[nr][nc] = dist[r][c] + 1.
Alternatively, two-pass DP: top-left to bottom-right, then bottom-right to top-left.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Shortest Path in Binary Matrix
problems.statement:
Given an `n x n` binary matrix `grid`, return the length of the shortest clear path in the matrix. If there is no clear path, return `-1`.

A clear path in a binary matrix is a path from the top-left cell `(0, 0)` to the bottom-right cell `(n - 1, n - 1)` such that:
- All the visited cells of the path are `0`.
- All the adjacent cells of the path are 8-directionally connected (i.e., they are different and share an edge or a corner).

The length of a clear path is the number of visited cells of this path.
commonMistakes: Forgetting 8 directions (diagonal movement is allowed).
Not checking if (0,0) or (n-1,n-1) are blocked upfront.
Queue shift() timeout on large n.
hints: First check if grid[0][0] === 0 and grid[n-1][n-1] === 0.
8-directional BFS: dr and dc each in {-1, 0, 1} except (0,0).
Mark cells visited immediately upon enqueueing to avoid duplicate states.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Number of Enclaves
problems.statement:
You are given an `m x n` binary matrix `grid`, where `0` represents a sea cell and `1` represents a land cell.

A move consists of walking from one land cell to another adjacent (4-directionally) land cell or walking off the boundary of the grid.

Return the number of land cells in `grid` for which we cannot walk off the boundary of the grid in any number of moves.

examples.explanation: Three 1s in the center cannot walk off the boundary.
All 1s connect to the top boundary.
Land cell on boundary can walk off immediately.

commonMistakes: Failing to flood fill connected boundary 1s before counting.
Checking 8 directions instead of 4.
hints: Any 1 that can reach the boundary can walk off.
Flood fill (sink) all 1s connected to the 4 boundaries by turning them into 0s.
After sinking, simply count the remaining 1s.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=35 for complexity verification

problems.title: Count Sub Islands
problems.statement:
You are given two `m x n` binary matrices `grid1` and `grid2` containing only `0`'s (water) and `1`'s (land).

An island is a group of `1`'s connected 4-directionally.

An island in `grid2` is considered a sub-island if there is an island in `grid1` that contains all the cells that make up this island in `grid2`.

Return the number of islands in `grid2` that are considered sub-islands.

parameterDefinitions.name: grid2
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n candidate sub-island grid

constraints: grid1[i][j] and grid2[i][j] are either 0 or 1.

examples.explanation: Three islands in grid2 are completely covered by land in grid1.

commonMistakes: Short-circuiting the boolean evaluation (e.g. `isSub && dfs(...)`), which fails to visit and sink the rest of the island in grid2.
Checking grid1 instead of grid2 in outer loop.
hints: Traverse each island in grid2 with DFS.
Crucial: Do not short-circuit DFS! All cells of the island in grid2 must be traversed and sunk even if one cell is already invalid.
Alternatively: first sink any island in grid2 that contains a cell where grid1 is 0. Then count remaining islands.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=25 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Where Will the Ball Fall
problems.statement:
You have a 2-D `grid` of size `m x n` representing a box, and you have `n` balls. The box is open on the top and bottom sides.

Each cell in the box has a diagonal board spanning two corners that can redirect a ball to the right or to the left:
- A board that redirects the ball to the right spans the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner and is represented in the grid as `1`.
- A board that redirects the ball to the left spans the top-right corner to the bottom-left corner and is represented in the grid as `-1`.

You drop one ball at the top of each column. Return an array `ans` of size `n` where `ans[i]` is the column that the ball falls out of at the bottom after dropping the ball from the `i-th` column, or `-1` if the ball gets stuck in the box.

parameterDefinitions.name: grid
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n board direction matrix

examples.explanation: Ball 0 exits at col 1. Balls 1, 2, 3, 4 get stuck in V-shapes.
Redirected left into wall, gets stuck.

commonMistakes: Checking grid[row + 1][col] instead of checking the adjacent column in the same row `grid[row][nextCol]` for a V-shape.
hints: A ball at (r, c) moves to (r + 1, c + 1) if grid[r][c] == 1 and grid[r][c + 1] == 1.
A ball moves to (r + 1, c - 1) if grid[r][c] == -1 and grid[r][c - 1] == -1.
If it hits a boundary or grid[r][c] != grid[r][nextCol], it forms a V-shape and gets stuck.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=50 for complexity verification

problems.title: Diagonal Traverse
problems.statement: Given an `m x n` matrix `mat`, return an array of all the elements of the array in a diagonal order (alternating between upwards-right and downwards-left).
commonMistakes: Boundary turning order: checking r === 0 before c === n - 1 when moving up-right causes index out of bounds.
hints: Elements on diagonal d have row + col == d.
When moving up-right: if c == n - 1, step down (r++); else if r == 0, step right (c++); else r--, c++.
When moving down-left: if r == m - 1, step right (c++); else if c == 0, step down (r++); else r++, c--.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=1 for complexity verification

problems.title: Search a 2D Matrix II
problems.statement:
Write an efficient algorithm that searches for an integer `target` in an `m x n` matrix `matrix`. This matrix has the following properties:
- Integers in each row are sorted in ascending from left to right.
- Integers in each column are sorted in ascending from top to bottom.
commonMistakes: Starting search at (0,0) or (m-1,n-1) where both adjacent moves either both increase or both decrease values.
Treating matrix as flattened 1D array (Search a 2D Matrix I assumption).
hints: Start at top-right corner `(0, n - 1)` or bottom-left corner `(m - 1, 0)`.
From top-right: moving left decreases the value, moving down increases the value.
This prunes an entire row or column at every step in O(1) time.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification

problems.title: Lucky Numbers in a Matrix
problems.statement:
Given an `m x n` matrix of distinct numbers, return all lucky numbers in the matrix in any order.

A lucky number is an element of the matrix such that it is the minimum element in its row and maximum in its column.

parameterDefinitions.name: matrix
parameterDefinitions.description: m x n matrix of distinct integers

constraints: All elements in the matrix are distinct.

examples.explanation: 15 is the min in row 2 and max in col 0.
7 is min in row 0 and max in col 0.

commonMistakes: Re-scanning rows and columns inside nested loops resulting in O(mn(m+n)) runtime.
Confusing min in row with max in row.
hints: Compute the minimum element in each row.
Compute the maximum element in each column.
Any number that belongs to both sets is a lucky number (at most 1 lucky number exists in any distinct matrix).

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=20 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification

problems.title: Island Perimeter
problems.statement:
You are given `row x col` `grid` representing a map where `grid[i][j] = 1` represents land and `grid[i][j] = 0` represents water.

Grid cells are connected horizontally/vertically (not diagonally). The grid is completely surrounded by water, and there is exactly one island (i.e., one or more connected land cells).

The island doesn't have "lakes", meaning the water inside isn't connected to the water around the island. One cell is a square with side length 1. The grid is rectangular, width and height don't exceed 100. Determine the perimeter of the island.
constraints: There is exactly one island in grid.
commonMistakes: Subtracting 1 instead of 2 for shared boundaries.
Missing grid boundary edges when checking adjacent cells.
hints: Each land cell adds 4 to the perimeter.
Each shared edge between two adjacent land cells removes 2 from the total perimeter (1 from each cell).
Iterate through grid: if cell is 1, add 4; if top neighbor is 1, subtract 2; if left neighbor is 1, subtract 2.

testCases.explanation: Stress test scale N=30 for complexity verification
Stress test scale N=40 for complexity verification
